findings.title: Talos describes malware C2 dead drops on public blockchains
findings.summary_md: This item covers Cisco Talos research describing operators that store encrypted command-and-control endpoints in Bitcoin transactions, EVM smart contracts, TRON wallets and Solana memo programs, then retrieve them with read-only JSON-RPC calls. It says blockchain-hosted configuration removes the single point of failure that domain seizure and sinkholing rely on. The piece recommends monitoring outbound JSON-RPC traffic and inspecting endpoint memory, and maps the behavior to dead drop resolver technique T1102.001.

findings.title: UAT-12643: Suspected North Korea-aligned actor blends blockchain resilience with targeted infostealing
findings.summary_md: This is a full mirror of Cisco Talos research on UAT-12643, a financially motivated cluster using the Go-based Overlord RAT, the Python Good Game stealer and a multi-cryptocurrency clipboard hijacker. It says Overlord hides encrypted WebSocket C2 URLs in Solana transaction memos and selects instructions whose data string is exactly 43 characters long. The report documents staging at 41.216.188.11, WinRE persistence through ResetConfig.xml and 35 RAT commands, with a low-confidence North Korea assessment.

findings.title: Talos finds UAT-12643 hiding C2 addresses in Solana transactions
findings.summary_md: AlCybr reports Cisco Talos' finding that UAT-12643's Overlord RAT reads encrypted command-and-control URLs from Solana transaction memos, so server addresses can change without updating malware on victim machines. It argues that on-chain C2 removes registrar seizure and sinkholing options and pushes defenders toward monitoring RPC traffic and outbound connections. The article also identifies the Good Game infostealer and a clipboard hijacker that replaces copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses.

findings.title: Don't Fear the Repo: UNK_DeadDrop Phishing Campaign Targets Developers to Steal Cryptocurrency
findings.summary_md: Proofpoint Threat Research describes UNK_DeadDrop, a likely North Korea-aligned cluster observed in April and May 2026 that sent more than 250 emails to nearly 100 organizations with developer recruitment and code review lures. The infection chain used attacker-controlled GitHub repositories, VS Code tasks and a malicious VSIX extension to deliver cross-platform loaders, including the open-source Go Overlord framework. The report says the operators targeted browser wallet extensions, decrypted credentials and desktop wallets, and tracks the activity separately from Contagious Interview.

findings.title: Suspected Norks send 250+ fake dev job pitches to steal crypto
findings.summary_md: The Register reports on Proofpoint's UNK_DeadDrop findings, describing more than 250 fake developer job or code review pitches sent over six weeks to people in almost 100 organizations. It says malicious GitHub repositories triggered editor tasks that installed cross-platform payloads, with Linux and macOS binaries based on the open-source Overlord C2 framework and custom modules for credential and wallet theft. The article notes that the Windows chain used a Node.js pipeline inside the editor's Electron process.

findings.title: EtherHiding & Blockchain Dead Drops: On-Chain Malware C2
findings.summary_md: Chainalysis reports a 5.2x year-over-year surge in blockchain-assisted cyberattacks and says nation-state operators from North Korea and Iran make up the majority of blockchain dead drop activity. It describes dead drops that store payloads or command-and-control data in on-chain transactions and smart contracts so campaigns survive domain seizures, hosting takedowns and repository removals. The post traces the tactic from Namecoin and Bitcoin OP_RETURN data through EVM EtherHiding to more recent state-linked use.

findings.title: Malicious PyPI, npm and RubyGems packages deliver Overlord RAT wheel builds and stealers
findings.summary_md: Corgea documents 13 malicious packages across PyPI, npm and RubyGems disclosed between November 2 and 4, 2026, including Overlord RAT wheel builds. It says the PyPI packages filipt, zyto and ln9qw38745g override the install command in setup.py to launch a bundled 33.1 MB Windows Overlord RAT executable during wheel building or installation. The research advises isolating hosts that built or installed the named packages and revoking sessions where companion stealers ran.
